stories.topic: Bell Labs: A Monopoly's Factory for Ideas
stories.summary: Asked where he would go in a time machine, Bill Gates chose Bell Labs in December 1947, the month the transistor was created. Bell Labs was AT&T's R&D lab, and by the 1960s it employed more than 15,000 people, over 1,200 of them PhDs. AT&T was a natural monopoly in telephony, so it had a guaranteed revenue stream and could fund research without chasing the next quarter. Amit notes the numbers are often overstated: about 2.8% of revenue went to R&D and only about 0.3% to basic research. What mattered was the long time horizon. Arthur C. Clarke described the New Jersey site as a factory for ideas. Ajay adds that Murray Hill had about 3,000 staff, roughly 1,000 of them PhDs, a budget many organisations in India could afford today.
stories.insight: Money did not make Bell Labs special. Patient horizons, culture and management did, and those can be copied by anyone willing to try.
stories.quote: But it is a factory for ideas. And so its production lines are invisible.

stories.topic: 'Hey, I'm Dick, Let's Go for Lunch'
stories.summary: In Kernighan's memoir, soon after he settled into his new office, a man walked in and said, 'Hey, I'm Dick, let's go for lunch.' Kernighan later realised this was Richard Hamming, whose textbook he had learned from. Thompson, Ritchie and other greats worked across the hall. Kernighan concludes that geography is destiny. Amit ties this to Shane Parrish's tweet on working from home. He also notes that many of the show's own best episodes, like Seven Stories That Should Be Films and the math episode, came out of unplanned in-person conversation. At Bell Labs no single boss controlled your career, and hierarchy was set by whom you respected.
stories.insight: Serendipity needs proximity. Going to the office is not about bureaucratic attendance. It is about the unplanned conversations where real creativity happens.
stories.quote: The idea is you need to interact with real people. Where the to me, where the real work happens, the real creativity happens is in the watercooler conversations. It's in the beer after the office work.

stories.topic: The Professor Who Forged Ken Thompson's Grad School Application
stories.summary: As a Berkeley undergrad, Ken Thompson worked on the university computer from midnight to 8 a.m., when he had the whole machine to himself. He called it 'my personal computer'. When a professor asked whether he would apply to graduate school, Thompson said no because he thought he wasn't good enough. The professor filled in the application, forged his signature, submitted it, and Thompson got in. Ajay tells a parallel story about his father, who went to night school and then did a master's in economics at Bombay University but got poor marks. The department's elders, D.T. Lakdawala, P.R. Brahmananda and M.L. Dantwala, knew him personally and took him into the PhD anyway.
stories.insight: Good institutions judge the person, not the cutoff. Ajay argues that India's habit of turning every decision into rigid black-and-white rules has thrown away useful discretion.
stories.quote: Because in India today everything is regimented and turned into black and white rules and we are opposed to all forms of discretion. And I think that somewhere in that we have lost the essence because actually we should always look at the person and not at mechanical procedure.

stories.topic: How the Telephone Company Tracked Down Ken Thompson
stories.summary: Thompson told Bell Labs he would never work for a corporation. They persuaded him to fly east and give a talk. Walking down the corridor, he saw the names on the doors and thought how amazing it would be to work near these people. Afterwards he drove to a friend's house, where Bell Labs delivered a printed offer, and then to a motel. Bell Labs phoned him there to ask whether he had accepted. When he asked how they had found him, they explained that they were the telephone company: they had called every motel in New Jersey until they found him. He accepted.
stories.insight: A cluster of great people is its own best recruiter, and a determined institution will use whatever advantage it has to win the person it wants.
stories.quote: And they said, Well, we're the telephone company.

stories.topic: Unix Was Born on a Junked PDP-7 in Three Weeks
stories.summary: After Multics failed, Bell Labs management refused to fund operating-systems research. Thompson grabbed an obsolete PDP-7 nobody wanted. It had about 16 KB of memory and a disk that was faster than the computer. He wrote a Space Travel game on it. Solving the disk problem produced a disk scheduler, a file system and a device driver, and he realised he was three weeks from an operating system. His wife and child left to visit family in California, so he spent one week on an editor, one on an assembler and one on the kernel, and Unix booted. The bare-bones system was named Unix as a nod against Multics.
stories.insight: Constraints and play produce breakthroughs. Amit calls it 'dancing with chains': a toy game on a scrap machine became the foundation of modern computing.
stories.quote: In every office, I think there is a suitable supply of rubbish that nobody is using. And I think this story runs contrary to any declutter manifesto that you do want to keep your PDP-7s because as you're going to see, they can amount to something.

stories.topic: Funding an Operating System as Patent Software
stories.summary: Management still refused to fund operating-systems work. But Bell Labs filed roughly one patent a day, and management was about to pay an outside vendor for specialised patent-typesetting software. The Unix team offered to build an in-house document system for the same money. They knew they would really be building out Unix on modern hardware. Management agreed. The result was roff, then nroff and troff, early markup typesetting tools. Ajay says the 'markup' in HTML traces back to this idea of commands embedded in text.
stories.insight: When the deeper bet you believe in won't get approved, attach it to a need the organisation already has a budget for. Doing real work under the official brief kept Unix alive.
stories.quote: For the money that management was about to pay somebody for a specialized piece of patent processing software, they were going to write an entire typesetting system, a document processing system, and run it on Unix.

stories.summary: Operating systems of the era were written in assembly language, which took someone like Thompson to pull off. Dennis Ritchie asked whether Unix could be written in a high-level language. None of the existing languages were good enough, so he and others built a new one: C. Then Thompson and Ritchie rewrote all of Unix in C, and it suddenly became portable to more and more machines.
stories.insight: Sometimes you have to build the tool that builds the tool. Ajay calls C, born to serve Unix, the most important programming language in the world today.
stories.quote: C was written to make it possible to write Unix in C.

stories.topic: How Antitrust Pressure Gave Unix to the World
stories.summary: Unix was far ahead of everything else, and AT&T could have launched its own computers and operating system and become a monopoly in computing too. Ajay thinks AT&T held back because it was fighting antitrust battles with the US FTC. Entering computers would have looked like extending its telecom monopoly. So it licensed Unix, source code included, to universities. A famous two-volume book printed the kernel source with a line-by-line commentary, and Unix became the common language of operating-systems teaching. At Berkeley, Bill Joy connected it to the networking work that became TCP/IP and the internet, and it then spread into Sun Microsystems and the wider industry.
stories.insight: An economic constraint, regulatory fear, turned a corporate asset into a shared global foundation. Ajay jokingly claims some credit for the economists.
stories.quote: I want to claim some credit for the economists here, that I think that there was significant pressure on AT&T at the time from the antitrust authorities.

stories.summary: In 1991 a young Finnish student, Linus Torvalds, posted on Net News that he had been tinkering with Minix code and had written a new operating system. The eminent computer scientist Andy Tanenbaum replied harshly. Ajay, older than Linus, thought Tanenbaum was being unfair and emailed Linus to encourage him. Ajay booted Linux at version 0.1. Apart from seven or eight years on Mac OS X, it has been his only system since 1991.
stories.insight: Revolutions often start as a student's hobby post that an established expert dismisses. A few words of encouragement to such a beginner can matter a great deal.
stories.quote: I thought he's not being fair and I was an older person compared to Linus. So I wrote email to Linus saying you should not be disheartened. What you're doing is very important.

stories.topic: Steve Jobs 'Got Religion' When iTunes Took a Week
stories.summary: At NeXT, Steve Jobs chose BSD Unix, and when he returned to Apple the NeXT team brought it in as Mac OS X. People Jobs trusted had long told him BSD Unix was the path to a great operating system, but he was taking it on faith. Then iTunes was written in roughly a week on the new Unix environment inside Apple. That was when Jobs is said to have understood that something magical was going on.
stories.insight: A good foundation shows its value in how fast people can build on it. That one-week build turned Jobs from believer to convert.
stories.quote: When iTunes got done in a week, Steve Jobs is said to have got religion.

stories.topic: The Bell Labs President Defends a Chess Program
stories.summary: During a demo for a powerful visitor, Ken Thompson showed a program that played chess. The visitor asked what use it was. Thompson had applied dynamic programming, the idea Richard Bellman and Robert Kalaba developed at RAND, to the chess endgame. Kalaba was Ajay's teacher, and Ajay's own PhD thesis on women in Malaysia rested on dynamic programming. Amit adds that these are now called endgame tablebases, and endgames with seven pieces or fewer are basically solved. The Bell Labs president answered the visitor himself: the work had produced algorithms that help schedule phone calls in the Bell system.
stories.insight: Play is a good use of a brilliant mind, and good management protects that play from demands to justify it right away.
stories.quote: It's such a great story about how building a space travel game and a chess program is actually a good use of the human mind. And the second, that this was understood by the management.

stories.topic: Aadhaar's Matching Problem That 'Couldn't Be Done'
stories.summary: Nandan Nilekani, Sanjay Jain and the Aadhaar team picked out one hard piece of the giant UID project. It had to match a person against about 1.4 billion records to catch fake IDs and remove duplicates. They asked the world's top computer companies and research groups for solutions, and several came back saying it couldn't be done. The team then built it themselves.
stories.insight: This is the Unix approach applied to public policy: find the hardest component and solve it first. Once it works, the rest becomes ordinary project execution.
stories.quote: They first tried to say some to somebody else, you do this, and then somebody else said, You can't do it. And then they said, okay, fine, very well, we will try.

recommendations.item: The Idea Factory: Bell Labs and the Great Age of American Innovation
recommendations.creator: Jon Gertner
recommendations.context: Amit's 'first recommendation of today', given while describing Bell Labs. The title comes from Arthur C. Clarke's description of the lab.
recommendations.reason: It explains how a long-horizon research culture at Bell Labs produced the transistor, Unix and much of the modern world's foundations.

recommendations.item: UNIX: A History and a Memoir
recommendations.creator: Brian Kernighan
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'a must read' early in the episode. Ajay names it as one of his three closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: An insider's short history of early Unix and Bell Labs. Many of the episode's anecdotes come from it, including Hamming's lunch invitation, 'geography is destiny' and Thompson's origin story.

recommendations.item: In the Beginning...Was the Command Line
recommendations.creator: Neal Stephenson
recommendations.context: The first of Ajay's three closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: It isn't an engineering book. Ajay says Stephenson, a great novelist, 'gets the dream, he gets the philosophy' of the command-line world and tells it passionately.

recommendations.creator: Eric S Raymond
recommendations.context: The second of Ajay's closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Ajay credits Raymond as the first to understand why open development works so well. A 'cathedral' is a few great people building something in one building. A 'bazaar' is thousands arguing in the open. The bazaar somehow produces the world's best software without paying anyone.

recommendations.creator: Don Norman
recommendations.context: A quick mid-episode recommendation during the discussion of elegance in engineering.
recommendations.reason: It teaches that everything beautiful is also beautifully functional, which applies directly to engineering.

recommendations.creator: Brian Kernighan and PJ Plauger
recommendations.context: Amit brings it up as an early programming book modelled on Strunk and White. Ajay later cites the link between the two books as proof that engineering and culture belong together.
recommendations.reason: It applies the values of good prose to code: simplicity, elegance, ease of understanding and no word out of place.

recommendations.creator: William Strunk and EB White
recommendations.context: Mentioned as the model for Kernighan and Plauger's programming book.
recommendations.reason: It is the classic statement of the clarity-and-brevity values that the Bell Labs community carried from writing into programming.

recommendations.item: Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers
recommendations.creator: Richard Hamming
recommendations.context: The textbook Kernighan had learned from before Hamming casually invited him to lunch. It is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It is the work of the Bell Labs giant behind the maxim 'the purpose of computing is insight, not numbers'.

recommendations.item: A Commentary on the UNIX Operating System
recommendations.creator: John Lions
recommendations.context: Ajay describes the famous printout of the Unix kernel source, with a second volume explaining it line by line.
recommendations.reason: It let universities worldwide study how a real operating system is written, which made Unix the common language of a generation of programmers.

recommendations.context: A credit-card-sized computer costing about 2,000 to 5,000 rupees for the board. The show notes call it the best bang for the buck.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says everybody should play with one. You boot Linux on it and start tinkering cheaply, whether with a keyboard, a thermometer or a plant-watering controller. Artists like Nomsita and Vaishnav could use it for art installations.

recommendations.creator: Linus Torvalds
recommendations.context: Explaining how 10,000 to 20,000 programmers worldwide coordinate on the Linux kernel in the open.
recommendations.reason: Anyone, including people in India or Bangladesh, can watch great programmers at work minute by minute and join in. You can start with a bug report or documentation and work up to writing code.

recommendations.context: Used in the screencast to turn his Emacs org file into a Word document for collaborators like Amit.
recommendations.reason: A 'Swiss army knife' that converts almost any file format into any other, and it is easy to wrap in your own one-word command.

recommendations.context: Ajay demos the plain-text file where he keeps future episode ideas, contrasting it with the cloud-based Roam Research they use together.
recommendations.reason: It gives a collapsible outline of nested ideas while keeping everything as a plain text file on your own machine, so grep, wc and other tools can work on it.

recommendations.context: Cited as evidence of how completely Unix has won.
recommendations.reason: Of the 500 most powerful computers in the world, roughly 490 or more run some variant of Unix.

recommendations.item: Shane Parrish's tweet on working from home
recommendations.creator: Shane Parrish
recommendations.context: Raised during the 'geography is destiny' discussion.
recommendations.reason: Its point, roughly that people who show up at the office will end up as bosses of those who work from home, supports Amit's view that creativity comes from in-person interaction.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay uses his own book to illustrate the Bell Labs culture of helping each other write.
recommendations.reason: He says it looks like he and Kelkar wrote it, but hundreds of people shaped it with ideas, arguments and draft reviews, including major improvements to the table of contents.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions that in his writing course he teaches the two-way link between clear writing and clear thinking. The show notes say registration for the Feb 2024 cohort closes that day.
recommendations.reason: Forcing yourself to write clearly trains you to think clearly, the same discipline the episode extends to programming.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled when describing great minds gathered in the Bell Labs corridors.
recommendations.reason: Bell Labs is a textbook case of the episode's thesis that great minds cluster and multiply each other.

recommendations.item: Seven Stories That Should Be Films (Episode 23)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Given as an example of an episode that came together on the fly while shooting in person.
recommendations.reason: It shows the creative energy of face-to-face collaboration.

recommendations.item: Math Is Better Than the Brigadier's Girlfriend (Episode 15)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned as 'the great math episode', also born from in-person conversation.
recommendations.reason: Another example of ideas that came from two people in the same room.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay jokes that the PDP-7 story 'runs contrary to any declutter manifesto'. He later notes that computers thrown out in decluttering can be revived with Unix.
recommendations.reason: Watching it alongside this episode gives a playful counterpoint: some of the junk you keep may become the next Unix.

core_ideas.concept: It's the Culture, Not the Cash
core_ideas.explanation: Many labs around the world, in India, the Soviet Union and China, had similar budgets and talent. Bell Labs stood out because of how it was managed. Power was federated rather than top-down, eccentrics had room to roam, and leaders didn't crave control. The postwar American counterculture, with its optimism and willingness to question authority, fed the same spirit that later flowered at Berkeley and Silicon Valley.
core_ideas.quote: So it's not the magic of resourcing. It is some other magic. It's a magic of culture, it's a magic of management and there is a lot for all of us to learn.

core_ideas.explanation: Bell Labs welcomed unconventional people with long time horizons but expected their ideas to become working things. That combination of eccentric freedom with a hard demand for real output kept long-term research from drifting into fantasy.
core_ideas.quote: In the sense that everything that was made was made with a purpose. Ideas had to become things. You couldn't just build castles in the air.

core_ideas.explanation: Kernighan's lesson from Bell Labs is that physical proximity to great people shapes what you become. Chance lunches, hallway conversations and beers after work produce ideas that scheduled interactions don't. Amit argues this is a case for in-person collaboration, not for showing up at the office as a performance.
core_ideas.quote: The idea isn't that oh you have to follow bureaucratic procedure and do the performative thing and go to office. The idea is you need to interact with real people.

core_ideas.explanation: The first system, like MIT's CTSS, is built by anxious mavericks working in isolation, so it is spare and coherent. Its success breeds arrogance and attracts power-seekers. They bring feature requests that are hard to refuse, and the second system, like Multics, collapses under overreach. Amit adds that Multics was trying to climb many trees at the same time.
core_ideas.quote: When they were doing the first system they were more human, they were frail, they were terrified, they were quaking in their boots. When the amount of boot quaking declined, hubris sets in.

core_ideas.explanation: Creative people always work under constraints, as Thompson did with his junked PDP-7, three weeks alone and no budget. Ajay's message to India is to stop imagining that top labs abroad have no politics or limits. C.R. Rao reached the frontier of statistics as an obscure student in Calcutta before email. Try to ease the constraints, but keep the curiosity going anyway.
core_ideas.quote: I just want to say that these chains are in your mind.

core_ideas.concept: Engineering and Philosophy Belong on One Shelf
core_ideas.explanation: The deepest engineering is tied to culture and aesthetics. Examples are the link between The Elements of Style and The Elements of Programming Style, and the influence of typesetting aesthetics on Steve Jobs. Ajay argues that India's split between the doctor-engineer world and the humanities has cost engineers their sense of what good engineering means.
core_ideas.quote: If you think the words culture and philosophy sit in a different shelf from the words engineering or science, then, you know, I would like to question that.

core_ideas.concept: Simplicity and Beauty as the Interface to the Human Mind
core_ideas.explanation: Systems built from a few simple components work better because people can actually understand them. Ajay cites David Gelernter's line that when faced with complexity, our only defence is beauty. Elegance is not decoration. It is how a limited mind grasps a large system.
core_ideas.quote: I want to use the idea that simplicity and beauty is the user interface of the human mind.

core_ideas.concept: Small, Bulletproof Tools Combined Like Lego
core_ideas.explanation: Build one small tool at a time with limited functionality. Make it well written, heavily tested and fast. Then build infrastructure so tools can be combined freely. This bottom-up approach beats top-down enterprise IT projects that throw thousands of programmers at one giant design.
core_ideas.quote: Don't ask humans to build a big giant complex system. Rather, go bottom up and build component, component, component. And then the humans will put them together like Lego blocks.

core_ideas.concept: Upload the Problem, Crack the Hardest Pieces First
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's personal method is to think about a problem for a long time without writing code, which he calls 'uploading' it into his brain. He then isolates the two or three hardest components and works on them with tunnel vision until they are solid. Once those are done, the rest of the design falls into place. The Aadhaar team's matching engine is his example.
core_ideas.quote: It's good to do one small component at a time. It's good to find the hardest things and solve them and get them done.

core_ideas.concept: Writing, Thinking and Programming Are One Craft
core_ideas.explanation: Good thinkers make better programmers, and good programmers become better thinkers. Code should be written for humans first. Donald Knuth wrote programs as essays interleaved with code, which his tools split into a book and a working program. The Bell Labs community wrote many books, took writing seriously and spent time improving each other's drafts.
core_ideas.quote: Writing code is like writing prose. They're not different. Okay, if you gentle reader think that you're writing code all day, what you need is to write more text all day.

core_ideas.concept: The Man Page Drives the Program
core_ideas.explanation: Bell Labs invented the terse, precise 'man page' style of documentation. Writing a clear man page forces clear thinking about what a program should and shouldn't do. It also invites sharper criticism than code alone. When the documentation starts to look messy, the program has too many features.
core_ideas.quote: The place to attack a program and throw out features is when its man page starts looking crufty.

core_ideas.concept: Tend a Garden of Fifty-Year-Old Trees
core_ideas.explanation: Much of modern programming means tearing down the house and rebuilding it again and again, because badly written code becomes unreadable within a year. Unix wins by improving mature code bases continuously for decades. That kind of building takes devotion, not sprints.
core_ideas.quote: We are building cathedrals. We are not in the stupid game of building a house and burning it down and building a house and burning it down, which characterizes so much of the modern computer programming world.

core_ideas.concept: Open Source Continues Five Centuries of Science
core_ideas.explanation: Sharing code is the same norm as publishing a proof: Newton gave proofs rather than asking to be believed. Bill Gates argued that software should be secret and commercial, while Richard Stallman argued it should be open like physics. The open camp won, even though Microsoft once earned most of the industry's profits and, in Ajay's view, produced no new ideas. Many competing Unix variants are a sign of healthy competition, since anyone can fork the code. Amit sees open source as another form of voluntary cooperation within markets.
core_ideas.quote: Like if I prove a theorem, I'm going to show you the proof. I'm not going to hide the proof. In similar fashion, if I write a computer program, I'm going to give you the code.

core_ideas.explanation: Once source code is downloadable, it is non-rival, because my copy doesn't reduce yours, and non-excludable. Unix and the internet received some public funding, including US Defense Department money for TCP/IP and AT&T's salaries for Unix. But they spread with no coercion and no national flag attached.
core_ideas.quote: There's no government in the picture, there is no coercion in the picture, nobody forced anybody. Okay, that is a digital public good.

core_ideas.explanation: Unix was built by clever people on underpowered machines with thin budgets, and its algorithms have been sharpened for fifty years. It gets more out of less hardware, so old computers headed for the scrap heap can be revived. The bar for algorithms in the Unix world is higher; quick and dirty doesn't pass.
core_ideas.quote: Whereas hiding inside Unix, there are extremes of nice algorithms where people have spent fifty years sharpening the algorithm, sharpening the algorithm, improving it, improving it, so that today it becomes a very efficient system.

core_ideas.concept: Freedom Is Built Into the Architecture
core_ideas.explanation: An operating system could easily impose tight central control. Unix and the internet were instead designed for free, flexible, anonymous use, with encryption and VPNs. Spam is a real cost of that openness. But the alternative, a world where Gates won and corporations or governments controlled all computing, would have been much worse.
core_ideas.quote: The internet is deeply wired for free, flexible, anonymous use. There is a great deal of anarchism. That is understood and accepted.

core_ideas.explanation: Keep data in plain text, not proprietary formats, so every tool can read and change it. The pipe symbol sends one command's output into the next. Commands like sort, grep, wc, awk, head and tail can then be chained into a single line, for example to find the show's three longest episodes or its minutes per viewer.
core_ideas.quote: Plain text files are the universal language by which all the programs speak to each other and are able to read files, modify files.

core_ideas.explanation: Unix blurs the line between users and programmers. Within minutes of chaining commands or writing a one-line awk pattern and action, you are writing real code. Saving a few commands in a text file creates a new command of your own, so automating your own work becomes a habit.
core_ideas.quote: That's a part of the Unix philosophy that generally we blur the lines between nonprogrammers and programmers.

core_ideas.concept: File Names and Folder Hygiene as a Superpower
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay keeps files that are thirty or forty years old usable through careful conventions. He uses logical names, underscores instead of spaces, lowercase for files, capitals for directories and a README in every folder for his future self. He treats this as a defence against a forgetful mind.
core_ideas.quote: Choosing good file names and managing a good directory system is a superpower and is an important part of being productive.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay on Amit's preparation: 'Gentle reader, this boy is not a Bengali dreamer. Look at the number of books he has read for this one episode. Get off your butt and read some books.' Amit replies: 'I am Bengali in the sense that I would urge my gentle readers, don't get off your butt. It's a very comfortable place. God gave you a butt for a reason, right? Actually God gave you a butt for two reasons. Both of which we are sort of indulging in.'
Ajay asks to 'show me where is the beef, or show me where is the rasgulla?' Amit: 'What you said was firstly anti-national and secondly unhealthy. No rasgullas, too much sugar. Cut to the chase.'
Ajay, to Indian nationalists who brand digital infrastructure: 'Nobody called it America Stack, they just called it Unix and the Internet.'

Ajay's dystopia without Unix's openness: a WhatsApp uncle insisting you do a UID iris scan every time you switch on your phone 'because otherwise terrorists will use phones', in a world where you are 'charged four rupees for each email'.

On Hamming's prediction that most of Bell Labs' work would become computation, Ajay says every sad graduate student now knows the truth: 'You may think you're doing biology, you may think you're doing political science... it's just programming.'
Ajay, a market-minded economist, prefacing his case for open source as a public good: 'So unaccustomed as I am to questioning some of the fundamentals of how modern capitalism works...'
Amit on open-source swapping: 'I give you my code, you give me your code. And obviously it's a win-win for me because your code is worth more.'
Ajay listing the devices with a CPU inside: 'inside every smartwatch, bracket, I have a dumb watch.'
Bill Gates, asked where he would go in a time machine, chose Bell Labs in December 1947, the month the transistor was created.
Arthur C. Clarke described Bell Labs' New Jersey site as looking like a large factory, 'but it is a factory for ideas', which gave Jon Gertner's book its title.
Richard Hamming, quoted by Amit: 'The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.'
Amit on writing as thinking: Deirdre McCloskey said writing is part of research, not something done after it, and Joan Didion said, 'I don't know what I think till I write it down.'
The rival manifestos of the mid-1970s: Bill Gates arguing that software should be secret and commercial, and Richard Stallman arguing that it should be open like mathematics and physics.

C.R. Rao as an obscure graduate student at ISI Calcutta before email, with 'no right to win', who still reached the frontier of statistics. Ajay's point is that even 'sitting inside a concentration camp you can write poetry'.

Ken Thompson's prophecy, retold by Ajay: somewhere a defunct Cray-1 supercomputer lies unused in a lab, a future Ken Thompson will write a space travel game on it, and the next revolution in computing will come out of that.
